title: How Pizza Meokda Grew to 43 Overseas Stores: K-Franchise Insights
description: Pizza Meokda runs 43 stores abroad and just signed in Uzbekistan. Three structural lessons on local partners, standards and post-contract management for HQs.
html:
We look at overseas franchise expansion strategy through Pizza Meokda's growth to 43 stores abroad.

43 stores abroad: the condition for expansion is an operating system, not a contract

CORE SUMMARY

✔ Pizza Meokda operates about 80 stores in Korea and 43 overseas, and has signed a master franchise agreement with an Uzbek company.

✔ The pace of overseas expansion depends on whether you work with partners that have local distribution capabilities.

✔ To stay steady as countries are added, menu, training and quality standards must be standardized.

✔ After the contract, the HQ system for managing store progress and operating history determines whether expansion is sustainable.

When a franchise brand expands overseas, the first number that gets attention is store count. But more important than the count itself is how that expansion was achieved and how it is managed after the contract is signed. According to a July 2026 report, Pizza Meokda operates about 80 stores in Korea and 43 overseas, and recently signed a master franchise (MF) agreement with an Uzbek company.

In this article, we examine Pizza Meokda's overseas expansion not through the outcome of a higher store count, but through the three structural features that produced it. We focus on strategic takeaways for headquarters considering overseas expansion.

Pizza Meokda's overseas expansion, by the numbers

Pizza Meokda is a brand with about 80 stores in Korea, and it was reported to run no fewer than 43 stores overseas. The small gap between its domestic and overseas store counts shows that the brand treats overseas expansion not as a side strategy but as a core pillar of HQ's growth strategy.

The recent master franchise agreement with an Uzbek company continues this trend. Under a master franchise model, instead of opening stores directly abroad, HQ grants a local company the rights to run the franchise business in a specific country or region. Because HQ does not have to build local infrastructure, legal processes or distribution networks itself, this model can speed up market entry, but how operating quality is managed after the contract becomes the key variable in brand credibility.

Taken together, these numbers and the contract structure suggest that Pizza Meokda's overseas expansion is not a one-off deal but a process of steadily growing its store count. In the following sections, we look at the three structural features that made this possible.

The small gap between domestic and overseas store counts shows how much weight the brand puts on overseas expansion

An expansion strategy built on partners with local distribution capabilities

Overseas expansion broadly takes one of two forms: company-owned stores opened directly by HQ, or a master franchise in which operations are entrusted to a local partner. Company-owned stores give HQ a high degree of control, but because HQ must build everything from scratch, including local legal processes, distribution and hiring, entry is slower and the upfront investment burden is larger.

Pizza Meokda's master franchise agreement with an Uzbek company can be read as a strategy to replace that burden with the local partner's existing capabilities. Local companies already understand the country's distribution networks, real estate and licensing procedures, so they can open stores much faster than HQ could by building everything itself. This is an especially effective strategy for brands that want to expand in several countries at once.

The risks of this approach are clear as well. If the local partner's way of operating deviates from the brand standards HQ intended, control can become difficult. So the success of an expansion strategy based on master franchise agreements depends less on partner selection itself than on how effectively HQ can communicate and verify its standards after the contract.

Leveraging a local partner's distribution capabilities can speed up overseas expansion

Standard operating criteria that hold steady as countries are added

The biggest risk in entering several countries at once is that the brand's quality and service standards are applied differently in each country. Consumers expect a similar level of taste and service from the same brand wherever they are, so if those standards waver, the credibility of the whole brand can suffer.

Brands that are active overseas often have systems for standardizing menu recipes, training programs and quality inspection criteria and passing them on to local partners. This goes beyond simply handing over manuals; it includes continuously checking whether local staff are actually operating to those standards. Since maintaining standards gets more complex as countries are added, it is important to establish clear standards from the early stages of expansion.

This kind of standardization is required not only for overseas expansion but equally for domestic franchising. Overseas, however, language, culture and ingredient supply conditions differ, so striking a balance between adapting standards to local conditions and keeping core criteria intact becomes even more important.

Standards that hold steady as countries are added underpin brand credibility

An HQ system for managing store progress after the contract

Management after the contract is signed is an often-overlooked part of overseas expansion. Closing a master franchise agreement is only the start of expansion; whether stores actually open and operate as planned depends on progress management after the contract. HQ must be able to see whether anything deviates from its standards while the local partner prepares store openings, and whether operating quality is maintained after opening.

Just as management gaps open up in domestic franchising when information breaks between the opening preparation and post-opening operations stages, overseas this problem can be much larger, compounded by geographic distance, time differences and language barriers. Without a system that lets HQ continuously check each store's progress, opening schedule and operating history after the contract, the number of contracts may grow while actual operating quality remains hard to gauge.

In the end, contracts drive the pace of overseas expansion, but whether that expansion is sustainable depends on how systematically HQ can manage store progress after the contract. This principle applies equally to every HQ growing its franchise network at home, not just abroad.

Managing progress after the contract determines whether expansion is sustainable

What HQs preparing to expand overseas should review

What brands active overseas, like Pizza Meokda, have in common is that they have an operating management system for after the contract, not just the contract itself. Selecting local partners, communicating standard operating criteria and managing each store's progress are not steps completed one after another, but elements that must be managed together throughout expansion.

HQs that have run many franchise stores in Korea will recognize that much of this management system overlaps with how they run their domestic franchise business. A system that manages consultation and contract history, checks opening preparation item by item, and continues to manage QSCV inspections and store information after opening is a foundation that applies equally to HQs preparing to expand overseas. Franchise-specific systems such as FDAM are built on these domestic franchise management practices, so HQs considering overseas expansion can use them as a reference for first reviewing their domestic operating systems.

Before preparing to expand overseas, the starting point is reviewing your domestic operating system

Frequently asked questions

What is a master franchise (MF) agreement?

A master franchise agreement grants a local company the rights to operate the franchise business in a specific country or region. Its advantage is that HQ can expand quickly by leveraging the local partner's distribution network and licensing capabilities without opening stores directly.

Why do standard operating criteria matter in overseas expansion?

When you enter several countries at once, the risk of operations diverging from country to country increases. Menu, training and quality standards must be standardized so consumers can expect the same brand experience in any country, which is directly tied to maintaining brand credibility.

Why does a post-contract management system matter?

Signing a contract is only the beginning of expansion; whether stores actually open as planned and maintain operating quality depends on progress management after the contract. Without it, the number of contracts may grow while actual operating quality becomes hard to gauge.

Before expanding overseas, review your HQ operating system first

The sustainability of overseas expansion is determined not by the contract but by the operating management system that follows it.
